name: Dark Beige
lede: Dark beige is a plain descriptive name, and one writer applies it to the natural color of muga silk from Assam.

sections.title: The color of muga silk
sections.body:
Finlay visits Sualkuchi, a weaving village on the Brahmaputra in Assam, where a weaver named Minu Kalita has worked at her loom for seventeen years [1]. Finlay says the muga thread first seems ordinary, and lists names for it that include Dark Beige, Tawny Mouse, Garden String and Wet Hay [1]. Muga cannot be dyed, so the brown thread always looks as it does now [1]. The cloth is woven for a wedding [1].

Muga is a wild silk, and Finlay notes elsewhere in the chapter that the village exists because of a 1603 edict by King Swargadeo Pratam Singh that required every household to spin and weave silk [2]. The color name here is only a description, but it points at a real thing: a fiber whose tone is natural, not dyed.

On screen the swatch is a muted tan, next to [[beige]], [[tan]], [[tawny]], [[khaki]] and [[dark-brown]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Dark beige is one of the commonest colors in our archive: it appears in 4,263 of 23,781 paintings, 17.93 per cent, more than 97 per cent of named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1400s, in 142 of 945 paintings, 1.4 times the museums' baseline [3]. Inside a painting it usually plays a light, in 45 per cent of the 2,613 paintings measured [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a yellowed varnish may push many colors toward this tan.
